Text, speech, and video are sequences, and their meaning depends on order and context. A fully connected or convolutional network expects an input of fixed size. A

instead processes a sequence one element at a time and carries a state from one step to the next, so that each output can depend on everything the network has seen before. This section describes the basic recurrent network, explains why it is hard to train, and introduces the gated cells that solved the problem and the attention mechanism that eventually replaced recurrence.

A recurrent network can map a sequence to a single output, for example a sentiment label for a sentence; to a sequence of the same length, for example one phoneme per audio frame; or, as the encoder-decoder below shows, to a sequence of a different length. A
network runs one recurrent network forward and one backward over the sequence and combines their hidden states, so that each position sees the context on both sides.

(GRU) of Cho and colleagues (2014) simplifies the LSTM to two gates, an update gate and a reset gate, and merges the cell state into the hidden state. It has fewer parameters and often performs as well.

architecture uses two recurrent networks. The encoder reads the source sentence and summarizes it in its final hidden state; the decoder starts from this state and generates the target sentence one word at a time, each step taking the previous word as input. A single vector must then hold the whole sentence, and translations of long sentences degrade. Bahdanau, Cho, and Bengio (2015) let the decoder look back at all hidden states of the encoder: at each step, it computes a weighted average of them, with weights that indicate which source words matter for the next target word. The transformer of 2017 kept attention and dropped recurrence. Its self-attention connects every position directly with every other one, so information no longer has to pass through a chain of hidden states, and all positions can be computed in parallel instead of one after the other.
